articles.title: Across 20 Spanish wind farms, stopping turbines when birds neared coincided with a 92.8% drop in recorded griffon vulture deaths over 13 years, with estimated power losses below 0.51%
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that temporarily stopping wind turbines near vultures drastically reduced griffon vulture fatalities by 92.8% over 13 years, with minimal impact on energy production.
articles.body: In southern Spain, researchers investigated a practical way to reduce these collisions: temporarily stopping selected turbines when birds were flying close enough to be at risk. Over 13 years, the approach was associated with a 92.8% reduction in recorded Griffon vulture fatalities, while estimated losses in electricity generation remained below 0.51%. According to a 2022 study published in Global Ecology and Conservation, a selective turbine shutdown protocol implemented across 20 wind farms in the Cádiz area of southern Spain was associated with a 92.8% reduction in recorded Griffon vulture fatalities over 13 years. The approach involved temporarily stopping individual turbines when birds approached at risk of collision, allowing the remaining turbines to continue operating.How the turbine shutdown system workedThis study involved monitoring 269 turbines located on 20 wind farms close to the Strait of Gibraltar, which is an important migration route for soaring birds migrating from Europe to Africa. The scientists looked at the rate of bird mortality during two years, namely 2006 and 2007, when there was no such shutdown protocol, and from 2008 until 2020, when the shutdown protocol was implemented.The observers monitored medium and large birds, especially birds of prey, approaching the turbines in situations likely to lead to a collision. When birds came too close, the observers contacted the control room to request a turbine shutdown. The approach relied on trained observers who could spot birds and recognise risky flight patterns. The turbines were restarted once the danger had passed, rather than being left off for long periods regardless of bird activity. This strategy mattered because bird strikes were not evenly distributed across turbines or throughout the year.What the 13-year study foundDuring the 13-year study, the researchers recorded 2,903 bird deaths and 354 bat deaths at the 20 wind farms. With the implementation of the turbine shut-off strategy, bird deaths among soaring birds such as raptors and storks decreased by 61.7%. The reduction was even greater for griffon vultures, whose recorded deaths fell from 12,627 in 2006 to 855 in 2020. These findings were notable because the vulture population increased during the study period. The griffon vulture population increased by more than seven times, and the number of shutdowns triggered by griffon vultures rose 2.5 times, from 3,517 in 2008 to 8,927 in 2020.The researchers estimated that shutdowns reduced annual electricity production by less than 0.51%. During the final three years of the study, turbines were stopped for an average of 108 minutes per intervention. Because Griffon vultures are active during daylight hours, the system could target periods of risk while allowing turbines to operate normally at night. Earlier research published in Biological Conservation also examined selective turbine shutdowns in southern Spain. That study reported a 50% reduction in Griffon vulture mortality during 2008 and 2009, with estimated annual energy losses of just 0.07%.Can selective shutdowns protect more birds?These results may help reduce the environmental impact of wind energy expansion. Rather than relying only on permanent restrictions or infrastructure changes, operators can respond to imminent danger by shutting down particular turbines if needed. Yet, there are some drawbacks associated with the method. It requires an observer to be present and able to identify danger in time to shut down the turbine. As the researchers pointed out, the procedure was mainly designed for large birds flying during the day.These findings come from a specific region where migration patterns, bird populations and turbine placement affect collision risk. Other regions may need different monitoring setups if birds are active at night or visibility is poor. Automated cameras and radar detection may help address these problems, but their efficiency and cost need to be assessed separately. Overall, the Spanish study suggests that selective shutdowns can help protect griffon vultures without major electricity losses.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Serial killer's ex-wife slept beside murderer for 8 years, never suspected his deadly double life
articles.summary: Bonnie Lou Gower reveals the haunting warning signs she missed while sharing a bed with serial killer Richard Evonitz for over eight years.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). For years, Bonnie Lou Gower shared a bed with a man she thought she knew better than anyone. She had no idea the man sleeping beside her was capable of murder. Her husband, Richard "Marc" Evonitz, was leading a double life, one that would ultimately expose him as a serial killer who preyed on young girls. His victims included a 16-year-old who lost her life while Evonitz was still married to Gower. SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED Decades after Evonitz’s crimes came to light, Gower is revisiting the warning signs she didn't recognize — alongside the young woman who survived him. In Investigation Discovery’s true crime docuseries "The Serial Killer Connection," Gower meets with Kara Robinson Chamberlain, who endured 18 hours of captivity and torture before escaping Evonitz, as they investigate whether he may be linked to other unsolved cases. For Gower, one question has followed her since learning the truth about the man she married. "When I initially learned about [his crimes] and I told people, honestly their first response is, ‘Well, obviously you knew. How could you not have known?’" Gower told Fox News Digital. "That was my very first question to the FBI. ‘How could I not know this? How could I not know I was sleeping next to somebody for eight and a half years that was doing this?’ And of course, they assured me that there’s no way I could have known." Looking back, Gower admitted there were things she didn’t question at the time. Whenever she left town to visit family, Evonitz insisted on staying behind, claiming he had to work. Only later did Gower discover that he had actually taken time off while she was away. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "One of the reasons he never came with me was because he said he was working," said Gower. "And then, I come to find out, he had actually taken off work on the days that I was out of town. But at the time, I wasn’t at all concerned about leaving him behind. I was just going and visiting my family. It definitely makes you look at everybody and everything now, whether you can trust someone’s words or actions." Gower met Evonitz, who was eight years her senior, in South Carolina. He was the older brother of one of her friends and would come home whenever he was on leave from the U.S. Navy. She quickly developed a crush on him as she got to know him and, at age 16, Evonitz asked her out on a date. They married in August 1988 when she was 17 and he was 25. "You think you know who you are when you’re 17, but I really don’t think I did," said Gower. "I don’t think I had a handle on that. And I was relatively sheltered. I was very naïve, very trusting, taking everything at face value. I think he knew that." During the marriage, there were moments when Gower suspected Evonitz was being unfaithful. Whenever she questioned him, Evonitz told her it was all in her head. She believed him. But as the relationship progressed, Evonitz began isolating her from friends and family as they moved around the country, from Maine to San Diego to Virginia. articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Iowans can't afford a soft-on-crime attorney general

articles.body: As an Iowa native, graduate of the University of Iowa and the University of Iowa College of Law, and two-time staffer for Iowa's senior U.S. Senator and Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, I know this for certain: Brenna Bird is the Attorney General Iowa needs reelected. Her Democrat opponent Nate Willems would be a disaster for Iowa, and the choice for voters in November could not be clearer. Since January 2023, Bird has served with distinction as Iowa's Attorney General. Her credentials are sterling: University of Chicago Law School, years as a prosecutor, county attorney in both Fremont and Guthrie Counties, and president of the Iowa County Attorneys Association — the highest honor a prosecutor can earn in this state. Today, as Iowa's Attorney General, Bird does not merely hold the office. She wields it as a force for justice. By contrast, Willems has never demonstrated the same seriousness. His legislative record and public conduct reveal a candidate soft on crime, hostile to the Constitution, and willing to smear American heroes for political points. The case sat cold for two years until Bird's newly created cold-case unit took it on. Within months, Karina Cooper and her lover Huston Danker faced arrest. A jury convicted Karina, and she now serves life without parole. Barbara Lenz, a 31-year-old mother in Woodbine, disappeared in 1989 after her abusive partner Robert Davis claimed he dropped her off. No body. No confession. Nearly four decades later, Bird's unit charged Davis. A jury found him guilty, and the judge sentenced him to 50 years. He will never hurt another woman. That is what a real attorney general looks like. TRUMP’S PUSH FOR NATIONAL CONCEALED CARRY RECIPROCITY WOULD PROTECT GOOD GUYS WITH GUNS Willems' record runs the other direction. Bruen. Willems also seeks to dilute Iowans' voting power by opposing voter-ID laws in a state with two swing House districts and recent races decided by fewer than a dozen votes. Comparing those heroes to an anarchist group responsible for widespread riot violence and attacks on federal officers is not edgy commentary. It is a moral failure. articles.title: Apple donations help Jersey cider festival go ahead
articles.summary: Jersey Heritage says it received around 40 bags of different varieties of apples from islanders.
articles.body:
Donations of apples have helped a cider festival go ahead after poor weather and heatwaves resulted in a severe fruit shortage for the organisers.

Jersey Heritage said its apple harvest had been badly affected , leaving far fewer apples available for its annual cider festival, La Faîs'sie d'Cidre.

The event at Hamptonne Country Life Museum on 17 and 18 October, recreates traditional cider-making using a horse-powered stone crusher and wooden press.

Nicola Lucas, Jersey Heritage's community events curator, said it had received around 40 bags of different varieties of apples, about a quarter of the amount they usually used, and were "really grateful".

Making the appeal for apples, Lucas explained the orchard normally produced about 80 large sacks of fruit for cider.

"We'll be lucky to fill two sacks this year and are also hearing that any apples that have been harvested are not offering much juice," she said.

She said donated apples came from islanders with one apple tree in their garden, as well as those who had a few trees or a small orchard.

"It's about a quarter of the amount we usually use but it is enough to demonstrate the traditional crushing and pressing of apples to make cider," she said.

Lucas said because this year's crop was not producing much juice there would not be as much fresh apple juice from the press for young festival-goers to try but they would still be able to watch the horse-powered crusher and wooden press being used.

She added: "Although we will be giving people the opportunity to taste last year's cider, some of it will be held back for 2027 to ensure that tastings can go ahead at next year's cider festival in the absence of a vintage from this year."

articles.title: In 1966, an Alaska dairy farm went up for sale; the community helped keep it off the open market, and it later became a 1,790-acre refuge visited by about 150 bird species
articles.summary: Discover how the Fairbanks community came together in 1966 to prevent a dairy farm sale, transforming the land into Creamer's Field Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, home to 150 bird species and an annual festival.
articles.body: Every spring, a large number of migrating waterfowl settle on open fields beside College Road in Fairbanks, in Interior Alaska. The fields were cleared for a dairy farm, and the 1993 interim management plan for the refuge, published by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G), notes that dairy operations began attracting migrating birds around 1910. The fields contained leftover grain and had been spread with manure, allowing them to thaw quickly and provide the birds with shallow pools of water and food before the surrounding landscape thawed.The people of Fairbanks realized that the roadside provided a clear view of the spring migration, and the local media covered it yearly, along with the breakup of the interior rivers. The yearly migration made the dairy farm a familiar feature of the community, and hence the news that the property was going to be sold posed a serious question about the future of the land. This problem was solved by volunteers, a family willing to wait, and state and federal funding. The state of Alaska acquired the fields, and ADF&G now manages them as the Creamer’s Field Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, as the same plan records.The dairy fields go up for sale in 1966The 1993 interim management plan for the refuge states that the dairy fields were put up for sale in 1966. Residents who valued the land as wildlife habitat and as open space for a growing city came together to find a way to buy it for the public. The Creamer family supported that goal and kept the property off the open real estate market while the effort took shape.A 1967 fund drive buys an option on the landBy 1967, the Alaska Conservation Society had undertaken a fundraising campaign to raise sufficient money for the purchase of the option to the fields. The option kept the land safe from being sold until the state obtained the necessary federal Pittman-Robertson funds and legislative appropriation for the purchase of some 250 acres of land. The strategy notes that the fundraising effort took place shortly after the Great Flood of 1967. The section on land acquisition highlights the purchase of the dairy fields in 1968. Next, ADF&G joined the Alaska Department of Natural Resources in making the 1,500 acres of adjoining state lands, together with the dairy fields, the Fairbanks Wildlife Management Area.From wildlife management area to state refuge, 1979 to 1982In 1979, a state game refuge was created by the legislature of Alaska for the location. The aims mentioned were the protection and improvement of the habitat of migratory birds, particularly those of waterfowl, and also for viewing and studying these animals. The dairy buildings were placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1977, and the state acquired them in 1982 along with 12 surrounding acres, as that plan records. The Conservation Fund describes the present-day refuge as roughly 1,790 acres. It also reports that approximately 150 bird species turn up there over the course of a year, including Canada geese, snow geese, trumpeter swans, mallards, northern shovelers, and sandhill cranes.The 1976 survey and the ponds built from 1984 to 1989A baseline for the refuge’s wildlife came from the Ecological Survey of the Birds, Mammals, and Vegetation of Fairbanks Wildlife Management Area, a master’s thesis by Michael A. Spindler completed at the University of Alaska Fairbanks in December 1976, as documented in the Alaska Department of Fish and Game’s interim management plan for Creamer’s Field Migratory Waterfowl Refuge. It is referred to as an inventory of the natural resources of the area, especially birds. The habitat enhancement came later. The neighboring property owner, George Dornath, constructed the first pond in 1984 together with the ADF&G. The department’s [hyperlink]Restoration and Enhancement of Aquatic Habitats report states that in 1987 ADF&G and Ducks Unlimited built six ponds at the refuge to increase nesting habitat for waterfowl. In 1989, a five-acre pond was put up, which was intended for sandhill cranes to have roosting areas in the summertime.Sandhill cranes, the airport and the banding projects of 1988 to 2007The crane pond grew out of a safety concern. Friends of Creamer’s Field, a nonprofit, recounts in Tracking the Northern Travelers: The Legacy of the Sandhill Crane Banding Project that airport officials asked ADF&G for help in 1987 because cranes were crossing the runways. Between 1988 and 1990, the biologists ringed 59 cranes. The banding project found that sandhill cranes feeding at Creamer’s Field in autumn also flew past Fairbanks International Airport each day on their way to and from nighttime roosts along the Tanana River, according to the Friends of Creamer’s Field account.The second effort involved 342 birds between 2001 and 2007. In 2001, four cranes were fitted with satellite GPS telemetry, and the data showed that they nested within 100 miles of the Tanana Valley and overwintered in north-central Texas. The management plan also says additional barley was seeded at the refuge while hazing and habitat changes at the airport aimed to make it less attractive to cranes and waterfowl.August crane counts and the festival that grew around themThe Alaska Department of Fish and Game recorded daily counts of migrating waterfowl and sandhill cranes at Creamer’s Field from August 1 to September 15, 2016, and reported them in its FY2017 Refuges and Other Special Areas Management Annual Performance Report. Crane and waterfowl counts at Creamer’s Field generally reached 1,500 to 2,000 during the last two weeks of August, and the Friends of Creamer’s Field article on the banding project lists peaks of 2,770 in 2002 and 2,575 in 2004. This aggregation takes place during the Tanana Valley Sandhill Crane Festival. The department’s [hyperlink] official festival announcement lists Friends of Creamer’s Field as the organizer, in collaboration with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, the Alaska Songbird Institute, and the Arctic Audubon Society.You use AI every day. articles.title: Reese Witherspoon sold control of Hello Sunshine at a $900 million valuation in 2021; five years later, she has teamed with Mediawan to buy the company back at a reported fraction of that price
articles.summary: Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine has returned to the person who built it.
articles.body: Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine has returned to the person who built it. In 2021, Candle Media acquired a controlling stake in the production company at a valuation of more than $900 million, a deal shaped by the peak of the streaming boom and the growing demand for premium, female-led stories. Five years later, Witherspoon has partnered with Paris-based Mediawan to buy the company back for a reported low- to mid-eight-figure amount, according to Axios.The turnaround highlights how sharply the business of entertainment has changed. Hello Sunshine remains a major creative force behind titles such as 'Big Little Lies', 'The Morning Show', 'Where the Crawdads Sing' and 'Daisy Jones & The Six', but its new sale price is only a fraction of the valuation it once carried. Deadline reported that Witherspoon is investing alongside Mediawan and described the acquisition as a homecoming for the company she founded in 2016.How Hello Sunshine built its reputationHello Sunshine began with backing from Peter Chernin and Jesse Jacobs through The Chernin Group. Its early focus was clear: create premium film and television stories centred on women, while also building a direct relationship with readers through Reese’s Book Club.The company soon developed a strong catalogue. Its credits include 'Big Little Lies', 'The Morning Show', 'Little Fires Everywhere', 'Where the Crawdads Sing', 'Daisy Jones & The Six', 'From Scratch' and 'The Last Thing He Told Me'. Those projects helped Hello Sunshine become one of the most recognisable independent production companies in Hollywood.Reese’s Book Club became equally important to the brand. Launched in 2017, the club reaches more than 6.2 million readers through its social and editorial channels, has driven roughly $900 million in United States book sales and has helped sell more than 60 million copies of its selected books in the country. More than 90 of its picks have reached The New York Times bestseller list.Why Candle Media paid so muchCandle Media was co-founded in 2021 by former Disney executives Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs. With about $2 billion in funding from Blackstone, the company pursued an aggressive acquisition strategy, gaining control of Hello Sunshine and buying Moonbug, the producer behind CoComelon, for nearly $3 billion.At the time, streaming services were competing fiercely for subscribers and exclusive content. That created a favourable market for companies with established intellectual property, famous founders and loyal audiences. Hello Sunshine’s mix of Witherspoon’s influence, successful adaptations and a highly engaged book community made it a valuable acquisition target.But the economics shifted soon after. Major streamers, especially Netflix, came under pressure from Wall Street to focus on sustainable profits rather than endless subscriber growth. As spending slowed, suppliers such as Candle Media faced a more difficult environment, while podcast platforms also reduced spending and made some of Hello Sunshine’s offshoot businesses harder to monetise.Why the buyback price is lowerAxios reported that Witherspoon and Mediawan bought Hello Sunshine for low- to mid-eight figures, a fraction of the more than $900 million valuation attached to the 2021 deal. The company and the parties involved declined to comment on the reported figure.The lower price does not erase Hello Sunshine’s creative value. It reflects a broader correction across the entertainment industry, where streamers have become more selective, media companies have pursued large mergers and smaller producers have faced pressure to reduce costs. Deadline noted that Candle Media’s debt burden forced it to depend on profits from its strongest properties, including Moonbug and ATTN:.Hello Sunshine had also begun narrowing its focus before the sale. Earlier in 2026, the founders of The Home Edit bought their company back from Hello Sunshine, which had previously tried to build a wider portfolio of media and lifestyle brands. The latest transaction signals that Candle Media is moving away from its plan to build one integrated media company and is instead operating or selling individual brands.Why Mediawan makes senseMediawan is a major independent content group with a global footprint. Founded in France in 2015, it now operates more than 100 production labels, including Kinetic Content, Wiedemann & Berg, Palomar, Drama Republic, Chernin Entertainment, Plan B Entertainment and See-Saw Films.Its catalogue includes internationally recognised titles such as Adolescence, Slow Horses, Call My Agent!, F1, The Greatest Showman, Love Is Blind, New Girl and the Planet of the Apes franchise. The group’s strategy is to bring independent production companies together while preserving their creative identities.For Hello Sunshine, Mediawan offers scale, international reach and access to a larger network of talent and intellectual property. For Mediawan, Hello Sunshine brings a distinctive creative brand and a direct audience connection through Reese’s Book Club. Mediawan chief executive Pierre-Antoine Capton said the acquisition strengthens the group’s ability to offer producers resources while maintaining their independence.What the buyback means for WitherspoonWitherspoon will remain closely involved in Hello Sunshine’s future. She said Mediawan has built a global independent studio by putting creators first, a vision she said has always guided Hello Sunshine. She also thanked Blackstone and Candle Media for their support and said the best is still ahead for the company.Hello Sunshine says it will focus on premium film and television and Reese’s Book Club, while exploring new storytelling formats and distribution models. The company also plans to use Mediawan’s international production and distribution network to connect with audiences around the world.The deal shows that market valuations can change dramatically, but a strong creative identity can survive a difficult cycle. Hello Sunshine may be worth far less than it was in 2021, yet its library, audience relationship and founder-led vision still give it an important place in the global entertainment business.You use AI every day. articles.title: Texas landlord kept a couple’s $2,600 security deposit and sued them for more money after they moved out; the tenants counterclaimed, won damages and legal fees, and the appeals court largely upheld it
articles.summary: A Texas landlord who retained a couple’s $2,600 security deposit and sued them for additional money after they moved out has lost most of her appeal
articles.body: A Texas landlord who retained a couple’s $2,600 security deposit and sued them for additional money after they moved out has lost most of her appeal against a judgment in the tenants’ favour. In a memorandum opinion dated October 15, 2026, the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals upheld the lower court’s decision in Yunan Angelina Zhou v. Adrienne Rawlings and Corey Rawlings, while correcting the calculation of damages and prejudgment interest. The dispute centred on alleged repair, cleaning, rekeying and painting costs, as well as whether the landlord had wrongfully withheld the deposit under Texas law. The ruling leaves the tenants’ main victory intact.Dispute began after the couple moved outThe case arose from a residential lease between Zhou and the Rawlingses. At the end of the tenancy, Adrienne and Corey Rawlings moved out of the house they had rented from Zhou. Zhou alleged that the property required repairs, cleaning, rekeying and painting after the couple left. She retained their $2,600 security deposit and demanded additional payment for the work she claimed was necessary. When the couple did not pay the additional amount, Zhou filed a lawsuit in justice court, alleging breach of contract and fraud. The Rawlingses responded with counterclaims, seeking statutory damages and other relief over the landlord’s retention of their security deposit.The dispute eventually reached Harris County’s County Civil Court at Law No. 2, where the case was heard in a trial without a jury. The court ruled against Zhou on her claims and awarded the Rawlingses damages under Texas’s security-deposit law, along with prejudgment interest, attorney’s fees, costs and post-judgment interest. Zhou then appealed the judgment to the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals.Why the security deposit became central to the caseTexas law places specific obligations on landlords who retain security deposits after tenants leave a rental property. Under Section 92.104 of the Texas Property Code, a landlord may deduct amounts for which a tenant is legally liable under the lease or for breaching it, but cannot retain money to cover normal wear and tear. The law also generally requires landlords who make deductions to provide a written description and itemised list of the charges, subject to statutory exceptions. Section 92.109 of the Texas Property Code provides that a landlord who, in bad faith, retains a security deposit may be liable for $100, three times the portion of the deposit wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney’s fees.Zhou challenged the statutory award, arguing that the Rawlingses had not provided a forwarding address as required by Texas law. She maintained that this failure meant they were not entitled to the damages awarded. However, the appellate court concluded that it could not overturn the trial court’s decision on that basis because the record was incomplete. Neither party had requested a court reporter to record the trial proceedings, leaving the appeals court without a transcript showing what evidence had been presented.Missing trial transcript weakened the appealThe absence of a trial transcript proved important to the outcome. Zhou argued that the evidence did not support the rejection of her breach-of-contract and fraud claims, or the statutory damages awarded to the Rawlingses. The appeals court explained that a party challenging the sufficiency of evidence must provide an adequate appellate record. Without a transcript, the court generally presumes that the missing portions support the trial court’s judgment.The judges also clarified that the trial court had not simply dismissed Zhou’s claims because there was no evidence. Rather, it had found that she failed to establish her claims by a preponderance of the evidence. Because Zhou could not demonstrate from the available record that the trial court’s findings were legally or factually incorrect, the appeals court rejected her challenges to the underlying claims and the statutory liability finding.Appeals court corrects damages calculationAlthough the court largely upheld the judgment, it agreed with Zhou on two calculations. First, the judgment had awarded the Rawlingses both the original $2,600 deposit and $7,800 in treble damages. The tenants agreed that this counted the deposit twice. The appeals court therefore modified the judgment to set the total damages award at $7,800. Second, the court agreed that prejudgment interest had been calculated incorrectly. It reduced the amount from $3,019.36 to $158. The court rejected Zhou’s challenge to the attorney’s-fee award because the missing trial transcript prevented it from assessing the evidentiary basis for that award. The court affirmed the judgment as modified on October 15, 2026. The decision preserves the tenants’ main victory while correcting the monetary calculations. It does not establish that landlords can never deduct repair costs; rather, it reinforces the importance of complying with security-deposit requirements and providing a sufficient record when challenging a court’s findings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amazonian wonder giant water lily blooms at Lok Seva Bhawan
articles.summary: Amazonian giant water lily (Victoria amazonica) blooms at Odisha Secretariat’s Lok Seva Bhawan, promoting conservation and research; public can view it on Republic Day.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: The next time you enter Lok Seva Bhawan, Odisha’s secretariat, a spectacular sight may catch your eye: A water body adorned with enormous circular floating leaves and fragrant flowers that change colour from white to pink. The attraction is the giant water lily (Victoria amazonica), an exotic aquatic plant native to the Amazon basin of South America, which has successfully bloomed on the premises of the administrative building.The initiative, aimed at promoting the cultivation, conservation and research of the giant water lily in Odisha, is the result of the efforts of Jayant Kumar Jena, superintendent of Capital Nursery functioning under the arboriculture wing of the general administration department, who became fascinated by the plant after meeting Dr R Saravanan, famous as Dr Shravan, a botanist associated with Botanical Survey of India (BSI), at Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden in Howrah, West Bengal. He is recognised for his conservation, propagation and public engagement work involving the giant water lily.“I was fascinated by the giant water lily after meeting Dr Saravanan at the Indian Botanic Garden in Howrah. I requested him to help us cultivate this extraordinary plant in Odisha. We procured a tuber and initially experimented with its cultivation on Capital Nursery premises in Unit-II area here. We succeeded in growing it, which encouraged us to take up a bigger project,” Jena said.He said the success of the initial experiment prompted him to develop a larger water body at Lok Seva Bhawan to facilitate the cultivation, breeding and research of the species. “After preparing the initial structure for the water body, I invited Dr Saravanan to Odisha to guide us. In July 2026, we planted four tubers of the giant water lily, including male and female plants. Three of them survived and grew successfully. Last week, we witnessed the blooming of the first fragrant flower, marking an important milestone in our efforts,” Jena added.The giant water lily is renowned for its enormous floating leaves, which can grow up to three metres in diameter. Their upturned edges give them the appearance of shallow circular pans, while a network of strong, air-filled ribs on the underside provides buoyancy and structural strength. The undersides of the leaves and their stalks are covered with sharp spines that protect the plant from aquatic herbivores.However, it is the flower that makes the plant particularly fascinating. Its blooming cycle spans around 48 hours. The flower opens as a fragrant white bloom on the first night, attracting nocturnal beetles that help in pollination. On the second night, it turns pink or purplish before eventually sinking beneath the water.Native to the shallow, calm waters of the Amazon River basin and the Guianas, the giant water lily has long attracted botanists, horticulturists and nature enthusiasts for its unusual adaptations and striking appearance.The initiative would help showcase the diversity of aquatic plants and encourage greater interest in botanical conservation and research. The cultivation of the species at Lok Seva Bhawan is expected to add a distinctive botanical attraction to the secretariat while creating opportunities to study the plant’s growth and propagation under Odisha’s climatic conditions, said Anjan Kumar Das, additional director of estate, GA department.Apart from pass holders and staff and employees, the general public also can witness the plant on Republic Day, when Lok Seva Bhawan garden opens for all.A group of forestry students of Odisha University of Agriculture and Technology (OUAT) visited Capital Nursery and was delighted to see and learn giant water lily cultivation on Friday. “Though I have studied about Giant water lily, I had never seen this plant. articles.title: Americans are secretly cooking during virtual meetings, with one age group leading the way
articles.summary: A new survey reveals 17% of remote workers have cooked during video meetings with cameras off, with Gen Z multitasking at even higher rates.
articles.body: Your colleagues might be chopping, stirring and whipping up a meal on the other side of your video call, a new survey found. A national survey of more than 2,000 U.S. adults found that 17% of respondents have cooked during a work meeting while their cameras were off, and among Gen Z, the figure rose to 26%. The poll, conducted by Savanta for AI meeting assistant company Bluedot, also found that 23% have used the bathroom during a meeting with their cameras off, 14% have shopped online and 13% have exercised. Twelve percent, meanwhile, have fallen asleep while their cameras were off, and that figure rose to 30% among Gen Z. BRINGING THIS POPULAR DRINK TO A JOB INTERVIEW COULD HURT YOUR CHANCES, EXPERTS WARN John Coleman, co-CEO of Atlanta-based Sovereign's Capital, told Fox News Digital he has occasionally resorted to eating lunch during back-to-back meetings and taken conference calls while exercising, with his camera off, but he draws the line at cooking while participating in a call. "I'd hate for someone to have a cooking accident while they're on Zoom and not be a full participant in the meeting," Coleman said. And some of the other behaviors are even riskier, he noted. "I had a colleague forget that his video was on and take his laptop into the restroom with him actually, which gave a great view of the restroom to everybody on the call, much to his chagrin," Coleman recalled. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ His tip is to treat video calls — on camera or not — as if you were face-to-face. "You want to be engaged with the person across from you," he said. If you need to step away and complete a task, he recommends sending a quick message to let the other people on the call know. Kristen Hadeed, a Texas-based leadership expert and author of "Human Leadership," said her company treats making lunch as "human time" — an everyday need employees should be able to handle. "These moments are part of life, and I want my team to feel empowered to take the time they need while maintaining open communication with the team." "When a person's time away from work will affect their availability, responsiveness or the team's ability to get work done, I expect that it is communicated so that we are all on the same page," Hadeed added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER For Catherine Fisher, LinkedIn's vice president of communications and a California-based career expert, the key question is whether multitasking affects someone’s ability to take part. "The question isn't necessarily, 'Are you doing anything else?' It's, 'Can you still contribute when you’re needed?'" Fisher told Fox News Digital. "If you can't follow the discussion, answer a question or contribute meaningfully, that's when multitasking can start getting in the way of your participation." Coleman said part of the problem is how some meetings are organized. "A lot of this responsibility, I think, rests on organizations," he said. "We overcrowd meetings. We make them too long." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS When employees feel they are not needed in a discussion, or that a meeting could have been handled by email, they may start multitasking, he said, and that erodes cognitive ability. Coleman recommends keeping virtual calls brief, limiting attendance to those who need to participate and asking whether a video call is even necessary in the first place. Fisher said the higher share of Gen Z respondents who said they have cooked during meetings may reflect how the pandemic shaped their expectations around work and home life. "Many started their careers during the pandemic, at a time when the boundaries between work and home had already been rewritten."

articles.title: ‘Cheap foreign labour’: US Congressman claims H-1B visa holders from India, China replacing American graduates
articles.summary: US Congressman Riley Moore has alleged that H-1B visa holders are replacing American computer science graduates, claiming employers are hiring foreign
articles.body: US Congressman Riley Moore has alleged that H-1B visa holders are replacing American computer science graduates, claiming employers are hiring foreign workers because they are willing to accept lower wages.In a post on X, Moore described the H-1B visa and Optional Practical Training (OPT) programmes as “SCAMS”, alleging that they allow companies to replace American workers with cheaper foreign labour.“H-1B and OPT programs are SCAMS that undercut and replace American workers with cheap foreign labor,” Moore wrote.He claimed that around 650,000 Americans graduated with computer science-related degrees last year, while more than 500,000 H-1B visas were issued.“We had about 650,000 kids, give or take, graduate with computer science, computer programming degrees in this country last year, and then issued over half a million H-1B visas,” Moore said during an interview with Scott Jennings on The Scott Jennings Show, broadcast by the Salem News Channel.“They're willing to do these jobs at a lower rate, cheaper labor, and so all of our kids are getting replaced in this,” he alleged.Moore questions H-1B visa programmeMoore argued that the H-1B programme, which is intended to help US employers recruit skilled foreign workers for specialised occupations, was not operating as originally presented.He said the programme was promoted as a way to bring highly skilled professionals into the country to fill positions that American employers could not staff with domestic workers. However, he alleged that companies were using it to hire cheaper foreign labour instead.“What it is, is importing cheap labor that is undercutting a lot of our young college graduates who are coming out of school with accounting degrees and other types of degrees, computer science, things like that, that are ready to enter the workforce,” he said.The congressman also claimed that H-1B visa holders bring family members to the US, linking the programme to what he described as “chain migration”.“And the typical H-1B visa holder, by the way, brings 10 individuals of their family with them. So you have this whole chain migration thing that goes with it,” Moore said.His remarks come amid continuing debate in the US over the impact of employment-based immigration on domestic workers and the technology sector.Proposed DHS rule could mean tougher H-1B extensionsSeparately, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed a regulatory change that could affect how applications to extend temporary work visas, including H-1B and L-1 visas, are assessed.The proposal seeks to remove a provision under 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) that requires US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to give deference to an earlier approval when an extension petition involves the same parties and underlying facts.Under the existing policy, immigration officers generally defer to a previous eligibility determination when reviewing a petition involving the same circumstances. Removing this requirement could allow officers to reassess eligibility even when an earlier application was approved under similar conditions.The proposed change has not yet been implemented. DHS is seeking public feedback on the proposed rulemaking package.Why the H-1B programme matters to Indian workersThe debate is particularly significant for Indian professionals, who account for a majority of H-1B beneficiaries. According to USCIS data, Indian nationals made up roughly 70 per cent of all H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal year 2025.For many Indian technology workers, the H-1B visa is an entry point into a longer career in the US. The programme allows American employers to hire foreign professionals for specialised occupations, including roles in technology, engineering and other fields requiring specialised knowledge.The annual cap for new H-1B visas is 85,000, comprising 65,000 visas under the regular quota and an additional 20,000 for foreign graduates with advanced degrees from US universities. Certain employers and categories of workers are exempt from the cap.Moore's claims that American graduates are being replaced by H-1B workers reflect his criticism of the programme and its impact on the US workforce. His remarks add to the debate over whether the system is helping employers fill specialised roles or placing American workers at a disadvantage.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: She was all in for socialism - until the 'red flags' became impossible to ignore
articles.summary: Germania Rodriguez Poleo warns young Americans that socialism and capitalism are mutually exclusive, drawing on Venezuela's collapse as proof.
articles.body: Germania Rodriguez Poleo, a Venezuelan-American journalist who emigrated to the United States when she was 11 years old, grew up to vote for Bernie Sanders in support of some of the socialist policies her family fought to escape — before she recognized what she described as the "red flags" of what she once supported. "Once I looked at the details, it looked more like Chavismo than Scandinavia[n socialism]," Poleo told Fox News Digital. Chavismo, a socialist program "characterized by nationalism, a centralized economy, and an active military involved in public projects," was named after autocratic leader Hugo Chávez, the movement's founder. "Ever since, I've been trying to share that message with fellow young people who truly just fall for the misinformation," she continued. SOCIALISM WILL 'CONTROL PEOPLE' AND 'TAKE EVERYTHING AWAY' FROM AMERICA, ACCORDING TO THESE EXPATS "[Venezuela has] done the suffering for you, we destroyed our country. Venezuela is an example for the entire world of how a democratic country can vote itself into total collapse… One vote was enough to lose our country, and who knows if we'll ever get it back," Poleo said. She went on to detail "the war over what the definition of socialism is," arguing that adding "democratic" before "socialism" creates a misleading distinction between socialist policies and the realities of life in Venezuela, Cuba and other countries. "Socialism and capitalism are mutually exclusive — and that's where [socialists are] lying to people," she continued. JONATHAN TURLEY: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS WANT TO REMAKE AMERICA IN THEIR IMAGE. THAT’S TERRIFYING "If you really talk to these DSA types, they'll admit it — they think capitalism has failed and they want to try a different system… That's [where] they're lying. Social democracy is under capitalism. Socialism wants to end capitalism and that is a very, very important distinction," Poleo revealed. "When did I open my eyes? When the red flags became too many," she added. She went on to explain how she came to support candidates like Sanders, touching on the "immigrant experience" and pressure to "assimilate" to the new Western culture that surrounded her. "It’s the same thing that's convincing young Americans all over the United States to view socialism favorably," she continued. OPINION: SOCIALISM LOOKS APPEALING WHEN SCHOOLS REFUSE TO TEACH ITS HORRIFIC, REAL-WORLD COST "By the time I got to NYU, and I had fancy professors telling me that the problem wasn't socialism, but capitalism, unchecked capitalism, repeating the horrors of trickle-down economics. [I was] going to classes like ‘the politics of inequality,’ ‘Latina feminism.' This is what was building my world view, all taught by White American professors, of course," Poleo recalled. "I ended up believing their lie that what they're talking about is social democracy, like in Scandinavian countries, and not what happened in Venezuela, Cuba, and Nicaragua," she continued. Poleo, the narrator of "Escaping Venezuela," a documentary by Reason, said that the lives, experiences and memories that encompass the stories of immigrants are "not convenient" for the people who support socialism. TODAY’S LEFTISTS ARE DANGEROUSLY WRONG ABOUT COMMUNISM. JUST LISTEN TO THE SURVIVORS "Our story and our tragedy is not convenient for people who say they care about victims of dictatorships or migrants… They don't like our story because it shows what happens in the real world when an anti-Western, anti-U.S., supposedly anti-imperialist government gets to power and establishes socialist policies," Poleo noted. "They want to say that's not real socialism, and they don't want to listen to us. I mean, they call themselves progressives while silencing the voices of the people who understand these systems the best," she stated. "I want young Americans, my fellow young Americans, to understand that Venezuela did not have to end this way… Listen to the victims. Don't insist [o]n the idea in the book that has never been put to work the ideal way that you're still waiting for. This is socialism. This is what happens outside of the utopia little book that promises equality… The examples are there. Stop looking away," Poleo said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
